trap.wrong: "Ask for 20% of every sprint for tech debt" or "we need a rewrite."
trap.why: Generic debt budgets get raided under pressure and don't target what matters; rewrites rarely get approved or finished. Debt work has to be justified by business impact.
trap.probe: Quantifying cost, tying debt to outcomes, and incremental delivery.
trap.say: "I'd quantify what the debt costs (incidents, lead time, on-call hours, blocked features), pick the items with the best return, attach them to roadmap work where possible, and deliver them incrementally with measurable results."

thesis: Tech debt gets prioritised when it's expressed as business cost and risk, tied to goals people already care about, and delivered incrementally with visible results. Treat it like a product backlog with a return on investment, not a moral argument.
pitch: I'd first measure the cost of the debt: incidents and their customer impact, on-call hours, how much longer features take in that area, onboarding time, security or compliance exposure. Then rank items by return: cost reduced per unit of effort, and risk of something serious. The best pitch attaches debt work to roadmap goals: 'the next three payment features all touch this module, and fixing it first makes them 40% faster', or 'this is the cause of half our incidents, which is hurting our SLO'. I'd propose incremental work, a strangler or refactor in steps, rather than a rewrite, with a metric to show improvement. Some debt doesn't need fixing: code that rarely changes and rarely breaks can stay ugly. A standing capacity allocation can work, but only alongside a prioritised, data-backed list so it's spent well.

points.d: Incidents, on-call load, slower delivery in affected areas, security and compliance risk, onboarding friction.
Effort versus cost removed and risk reduced; fix high-interest debt first.
Frame debt work as enabling upcoming features or meeting reliability targets.
Small steps with metrics (incident rate, lead time) rather than big-bang rewrites.
Stable, rarely changed code isn't worth refactoring just for neatness.
A debt register with owners and costs, reviewed with product partners.

decision: Prioritise debt with the highest business cost per unit of effort, bundle it with related feature work, and show results with metrics to earn more investment.
numbers: Example case: a flaky deploy pipeline costing 6 engineer-hours per week across a team is about 300 hours a year; a 3-week fix pays back within months.
pitfalls: Moral arguments ('the code is bad') instead of business ones.
Debt time with no prioritised list, spent on pet projects.
Never measuring results, so the next request is harder.

followups.q: Product says features always come first. What do you do?
followups.a: Show the features being slowed or the incidents hurting customers, and propose the smallest debt fix that unblocks the next feature.

followups.q: How do you measure that debt work paid off?
followups.a: Compare before and after: incident counts, lead time for changes in the area, on-call pages, or build times.
Rarely: when the platform is end-of-life or fundamentally can't meet requirements, and even then via incremental strangler migration.

example: A team showed that 45% of payment incidents traced to one legacy reconciliation module and that two roadmap features needed changes there. Product agreed to a six-week incremental refactor bundled with the first feature; incidents in that area dropped 70% the next quarter.

sources.title: Will Larson: Migrations, the sole scalable fix to tech debt
